AI is transforming the world. In this guest article, ShareAction explains how, in response, charities can unleash the positive potential of their AI investments

Sensitive content: Includes themes of sexual violence

Imagine this: you’ve spent hours and hours working on your charity’s AI strategy. You now know your ChatGPT from your Claude. You understand how it can be applied in your day-to-day – and where it might be best avoided. You might have even started to address some of the risks of AI, from social inequality to environmental pollution, through your grant-making or programme of services.

But there’s something lurking in your investments. There’s a good chance some of that money is tied up in AI, meaning there’s a risk that your organisation’s investments could be working against your mission in ways you haven’t considered.

Squaring this circle might feel impossible, but there are ways that charities can put their rights as investors in AI companies to good use.

The growth of companies developing, supporting, or deploying AI has boomed in recent years. There is no doubt about it: AI is transforming everything from the way that we plan our meals to deep scientific and academic research. But it’s also posing a whole new set of risks to society and the environment.

Public backlash about the environmental impacts of AI data centres is all over the news. The concerns are very real – over “100 new data centres in the UK will burn gas to generate electricity”, threatening the country’s climate goals, while the UK Government is failing to accommodate data centres’ water demands.

And after a summer of heatwaves, concerns about climate change have never been higher, so it’s unsurprising that communities are pushing back on data centre build-out for AI. Many AI companies will claim that their technologies will provide environmental benefits that outweigh their damaging impact to our climate, but the evidence disagrees.

AI also poses worrying threats to its users. The National Crime Agency has released guidance for parents warning them not to share images of their children online due to the growing threat of AI-generated videos of child sexual abuse, while UN Women has warned that the technology is reproducing gender stereotypes and racial bias.

As investors, charities need to understand which companies they hold investments in and the impacts those companies have on people all around the world.

If you’re an environmental charity cleaning up our polluted and heat-strained water ways, are the companies responsible for the data centre boom aligned with your values? Or as a children’s rights charity, does investing in the technology that produced sexual images of children align with your mission?

This isn’t an argument for charities and foundations to immediately drop their investments; there is an important role for these organisations to play as morally driven investors. By exercising the rights that come with being a shareholder, charities can hold AI companies to account for the risks they pose to their missions.

Building your understanding of the risks that AI poses and thinking about how they relate to your mission is a strong place to start. Those considerations can then be embedded in your investment policy, as investors such as the pension fund Nest have begun to do.

Find out what your asset manager is doing to mitigate AI risks. How do they plan to vote on shareholder resolutions and director re-elections at companies that continue to have impacts on people and places that are core to your mission? The secretariat for the Charities Responsible Investment Network has produced a brief for charities on the climate impact of AI investments, which includes a list of questions you can ask your asset manager.

You might encounter some pushback. But charities have a unique power as investors – your voice carries moral authority and public respect that you can wield. And if your asset manager isn’t responding to your concerns, make it clear that you’re willing to move your mandate.

Working alongside other investors, you can amplify your impact. Organisations like the World Benchmarking Alliance and Thomson Reuters Foundation are already convening investors on AI and climate concerns.

Big pension funds like RailPen, CalPERS and Nest are already leading the way on AI governance, demonstrating how to navigate holding and divesting AI investments in ways that reflect their values and missions.

And Majority Action, a non-profit that works with investors on corporate accountability, has produced guidance for investors on mitigating AI risks by voting against the re-election of directors to express dissatisfaction. There’s a range of guidance with examples and inspiration for investors looking to get started.

Investors have successfully pushed for change on climate concerns by exercising their shareholder rights. In 2023, French bank BNP Paribas strengthened its oil and gas policy twice in three months following engagement from ShareAction and investors.

As morally driven, bold organisations with public profiles, charities must be aware of the risks that their AI investments pose. These risks might just be working against their very missions. By engaging with these companies as informed, bold shareholders, charities can wield their investments to further their goals instead.

At ShareAction we work to define the highest standards for responsible investment and to drive change until these standards are adopted worldwide. In doing so, we aim to harness the power of the financial system to tackle the biggest environmental and social challenges we face.

ShareAction hosts the secretariat for the Charities Responsible Investment Network (CRIN). Through CRIN, we support charities and foundations to navigate issues like this. Find out more about our collaborative group of investors working to align their investments with their missions below.
